chunks.text: 2 Methods 2.1 Cohorts and endpoint The primary cohort included 210 TCGA-KIRC patients with histopathology images, CT scans, and disease-specific survival (DSS) labels from TCGA-CDR [ 5 ] . The cohort included 46 DSS events with median follow-up of 3.7 years. Patients with missing or invalid outcomes or an empty mask were excluded, as were frozen sections. Imaging models used no clinical covariates. For external evaluation, we used PANTHER’s CPTAC-CCRCC test list comprising 180 patients and 341 tumor slides, with 15 DSS events, 26 overall-survival (OS) events, and median follow-up of 2.5 years [ 6 ] . Since only one DSS event occurred among the 52 patients with CT, external testing withheld CT. Adding 291 histology-only TCGA patients expanded training for this experiment to 501 patients with 109 DSS events. Slides were pooled per patient for external training and testing. 2.2 Histology prototypes and anatomical CT tokens Frozen UNI2-h [ 7 ] encoded 256 × 256 256\times 256 -pixel tissue patches at 20 × 20\times into 1,536-dimensional embeddings, yielding approximately 6,300 patches per slide. Following PANTHER [ 1 ] , we initialized 16 shared prototypes using k k -means on 100,000 TCGA patches and fitted a patient-specific diagonal Gaussian mixture with one expectation–maximization iteration. Each prototype produced 𝐡 k = [ log ⁡ ( π k + 10 − 4 ) , 𝝁 k , 𝝈 k 2 ] ∈ ℝ 3073 , \mathbf{h}_{k}=[\log(\pi_{k}+10^{-4}),\boldsymbol{\mu}_{k},\boldsymbol{\sigma}_{k}^{2}]\in\mathbb{R}^{3073}, (1) encoding prevalence, mean appearance, and variability. Shared initialization established corresponding prototype slots across patients. The label-free dictionary was shared across TCGA folds and fixed for CPTAC. For each patient, we selected one axial CT series from the earliest eligible study, prioritizing nephrographic or portal venous contrast phases. Eligible series contained ≥ 20 \geq 20 slices with spacing ≤ 5 \leq 5 mm and coverage ≥ 100 \geq 100 mm.

Volumes were oriented superior–posterior–left, resampled to 3 × 1 × 1 3\times 1\times 1 mm, and scaled from [ − 1024 , 2048 ] [-1024,2048] HU to [ 0 , 1 ] [0,1] . BAMF masks defined a kidney-region box with a 30 mm margin around retained components of ≥ 10 \geq 10 ml within a 250 mm superior–inferior span. Tumor labels were not supplied as predictive features. Frozen CT-FM [ 8 ] encoded the padded box in one pass. Adaptive pooling of its final 512-channel feature map onto a 2 × 4 × 4 2\times 4\times 4 grid produced M ≤ 32 M\leq 32 tokens 𝐜 j ∈ ℝ 512 \mathbf{c}_{j}\in\mathbb{R}^{512} , with centers expressed relative to the kidney-mask centroid in 100 mm units. All feature standardization used training-fold statistics. Figure 2: (A) Out-of-fold histology/CT risk percentiles, colored by fusion percentile; triangles denote DSS deaths. (B) In-sample IG decomposition into reference and modality contributions. (C) Prototype scores: red raises risk and blue lowers it. 2.3 Bidirectional fusion and survival learning We projected both token sets to d = 64 d=64 , adding learned prototype embeddings for histology and linearly embedded three-dimensional positions for CT. Each stream passed through one pre-normalized self-attention layer with four heads, feed-forward width 128, GELU activation, and dropout 0.25. Bidirectional cross-attention then updated the streams according to X m ← X m + MHA m ← n ⁡ ( X ¯ m , X ¯ n , X ¯ n ) , X_{m}\leftarrow X_{m}+\operatorname{MHA}_{m\leftarrow n}(\bar{X}_{m},\bar{X}_{n},\bar{X}_{n}), (2) where X ¯ = LN ⁡ ( X ) \bar{X}=\operatorname{LN}(X) , LN denotes layer normalization, and MHA denotes multi-head attention. The pairs ( m , n ) ∈ { ( h , c ) , ( c , h ) } (m,n)\in\{(h,c),(c,h)\} represent the two directions between histology ( h h ) and CT ( c c ), with separate directional weights and CT padding masks.

Following residual feed-forward updates, mean-pooled histology and gated-attention-pooled CT [ 9 ] were concatenated into a 128-dimensional representation and linearly mapped to risk r i r_{i} . Training minimized the event-averaged negative Cox partial log-likelihood with Breslow handling of ties, ℒ = − 1 N e ∑ ℓ [ ∑ i ∈ D ℓ r i − | D ℓ | log ∑ j | T j ≥ t ℓ e r j ] , \mathcal{L}=-\frac{1}{N_{e}}\sum_{\ell}\left[\sum_{i\in D_{\ell}}r_{i}-|D_{\ell}|\log\!\sum_{j\,\mid\,T_{j}\geq t_{\ell}}e^{r_{j}}\right], (3) where D ℓ D_{\ell} contains patients with events at distinct time t ℓ t_{\ell} , T j T_{j} is the observed follow-up time, and N e N_{e} is the total event count. Training-only modality dropout withheld CT or histology with probability 0.15, disabling that modality’s contribution to the other stream and zeroing its pooled representation. CT was withheld when unavailable, and both image encoders remained frozen. 2.4 Comparators and evaluation We compared fusion against unimodal token models with linear heads and a histology MLP using log mixture weights and their weighted mean. Early fusion concatenated these histology features with pooled CT (2,064-D), followed by ridge Cox regression or a 32-unit MLP. Ridge penalties were tuned over { 10 − 3 , 10 − 2 , 10 − 1 , 1 , 10 } \{10^{-3},10^{-2},10^{-1},1,10\} using inner five-fold CV. Late fusion averaged standardized risks from independently trained token models. All models used identical event-stratified five-fold splits. Neural models trained for 40 full-batch epochs across three seeds with AdamW and gradient clipping at 1. Learning rates and weight decay were ( 3 × 10 − 4 , 10 − 2 ) (3\times 10^{-4},10^{-2}) for token models and ( 10 − 4 , 0.1 ) (10^{-4},0.1) for MLPs. Per-seed risks were standardized against training predictions before averaging. Design screening used a separate five-repeat, five-fold protocol.

We reported fold-wise Harrell’s concordance (C-index) and three-year cumulative/dynamic AUROC and sensitivities at 80% and 90% specificity from pooled out-of-fold risks with inverse-probability-of-censoring weighting. Three-year events were cases, follow-up beyond three years defined controls, and earlier censorings were excluded (31 cases, 126 controls). Intervals used 1,000 patient-level bootstrap resamples. Thresholds derived from evaluation controls yielded descriptive ROC operating points. 2.5 Attribution analysis Integrated gradients (IG) [ 10 ] explained the standardized three-seed risk from a model fitted to all 210 patients. The baseline replaced token content with cohort averages while retaining patient-specific CT positions and token count. A 64-step right-Riemann approximation yielded modality-, prototype-, and CT-token attributions with median absolute completeness error of 0.0026. To visualize histology contributions, prototype scores were distributed over patches using Gaussian-mixture posteriors and spatially aggregated. The resulting maps represent prototype projections rather than patch-level IG. Attributions were in-sample, whereas risk percentiles were out-of-fold. Table 1: DSS concordance comparison. Small residuals reflect rounding and numerical integration. 3.1 Fusion performance on a common cohort On the common cohort, cross-attention fusion achieved the highest mean C-index ( 0.760 ± 0.081 0.760\pm 0.081 ), three-year AUROC (0.773), and sensitivity at 80% specificity (0.603), alongside the lowest C-index SD (Table 2 ). At 90% specificity, sensitivities were similar across nonlinear fusion designs (0.440–0.448). Although fusion increased mean concordance over histology MLP, histology tokens, and CT by 0.030, 0.054, and approximately 0.090, the corresponding paired intervals of [ − 0.151 , 0.211 ] [-0.151,0.211] , [ − 0.104 , 0.212 ] [-0.104,0.212] , and [ − 0.086 , 0.265 ] [-0.086,0.265] included zero and did not establish superiority. 3.2 External histology-pathway evaluation With CT withheld, the fusion model yielded external DSS C-index of 0.629 [0.434, 0.816], compared with 0.552 [0.339, 0.751] for histology tokens and 0.554 [0.403, 0.718] for histology MLP. This result followed expansion of TCGA training from 210 to 501 patients, which increased external DSS C-index from 0.541 to 0.629. Exploratory OS C-index was 0.674 [0.541, 0.789]. 3.3 From patient ranking to image evidence Fusion re-ranked two representative cases (Fig. 2 A): a grade-4 patient who died at 0.3 years rose from the 49th (histology-only) and 82nd (CT-only) percentiles to the 86th, and a grade-3 patient event-free at 5.6 years fell from the 27th and 38th to the 15th.

Fused risk rose from − 0.47 -0.47 to + 1.92 +1.92 through histology ( + 1.58 +1.58 ) and CT ( + 0.81 +0.81 ) in the high-risk case, while low-risk contributions were near zero ( − 0.05 -0.05 , − 0.01 -0.01 ; Fig. 2 B). Unimodal models assigned larger CT ( + 2.33 +2.33 ) and low-risk histology ( − 0.93 -0.93 ) contributions (Fig. 3 ), suggesting fusion redistributes evidence across modalities. Histology provided a median 77% (IQR 62–87%) of absolute cohort IG; CT contributions concentrated on the tumor side, and histology maps exposed potential pen/scanner shortcuts. 3.2 External histology-pathway evaluation With CT withheld, the fusion model yielded external DSS C-index of 0.629 [0.434, 0.816], compared with 0.552 [0.339, 0.751] for histology tokens and 0.554 [0.403, 0.718] for histology MLP. This result followed expansion of TCGA training from 210 to 501 patients, which increased external DSS C-index from 0.541 to 0.629. Exploratory OS C-index was 0.674 [0.541, 0.789]. 4 Discussion Preserving within-modality structure while enabling cross-modal interaction yielded the highest mean DSS performance among evaluated designs. Although weaker alone, CT improved fusion performance beyond histology, highlighting its complementary value. Our approach integrates CT spatial information with histology prototype appearance and variability, extending cross-scale fusion [ 1 , 2 , 3 , 4 ] . PANTHER Top + linear achieved 0.741 on TCGA, while All + MLP achieved 0.691 on CPTAC, exceeding our CT-hidden external mean of 0.629 as seen from Table 1 . However, differences in cohorts, encoders, splits, and uncertainty estimates prevent direct superiority claims. Limited DSS events (46 internally and 15 externally) and wide intervals constrain inference. Differences in representations and training warrant matched cross-attention ablations.

Screening-informed selection and a shared unlabeled dictionary may introduce optimism, while strong hospital signals in histology embeddings motivate site-held-out evaluation. Pen and scanner artifacts remained accessible to the model despite display filtering. Automatic masks and in-sample, baseline-dependent attributions further limit biological interpretation. External validation lacked CT, while calibration and incremental value beyond stage-inclusive clinical models remain untested. Future work should prioritize independent paired-modality validation, artifact removal, fold-specific prototypes, and matched ablations. 5 Conclusion Cross-attention fusion achieved the highest average DSS performance among evaluated designs. Attribution revealed complementary image contributions and artifacts, motivating independent multimodal validation.
